--- title: "Lab 6: Maxent" subtitle: "FW 532 · Python version" --- **Goals:** To get familiar with Maxent, run some models in Java and Python, and look at sensitivity to some of the parameters. **You Will Need:** * The course environmental raster stack (`data/envStack.tif`, included in the starter kit) * The Maxent Java application (see below; it needs Java installed on your computer) * Python packages: numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn, rasterio, elapid (see `requirements.txt`) * The course helper module `sdmlab.py` (in the same folder as this notebook) Remember to run the cells in order from top to bottom. Download Maxent version 3.4.4 [here](https://biodiversityinformatics.amnh.org/open_source/maxent/). We will be working largely from the Maxent [tutorial](https://biodiversityinformatics.amnh.org/open_source/maxent/Maxent_tutorial_2021.pdf). In this lab, you will generate data similarly to the other labs, and model it with the Maxent software following the steps in the tutorial. That is, you will replicate the steps of the tutorial using your own simulated data instead of (or in addition to) the data provided with the tutorial. > **Using Colab?** The Maxent Java app runs on your own computer, not in Colab. If you run this > notebook in Colab, download the files it writes (the `output/lab06` folder, see below) to your > computer before you start the Java part. ::: {#db4d08e7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Running on Google Colab? This cell downloads the course files. (Anywhere else it does nothing.) import os, sys if "google.colab" in sys.modules: if not os.path.exists("/content/fw532"): !git clone -q --depth 1 https://github.com/Hutchinson-Lab/fw532.git /content/fw532 %pip install -q rasterio elapid os.chdir("/content/fw532/python") ``` ::: ::: {#57231358 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score import elapid # Maxent in Python import sdmlab as sdm # course helpers for rasters ``` ::: # Generate Data This section is almost identical to our data generation from the early labs with the linear functions of covariates. The main difference is that we will only keep the presence points we generate, since we are simulating presence-only data. We will write these locations out to a file to be loaded into Maxent. We will also convert our environmental layers to ascii instead of tif format for Maxent. Set-up: everything this lab writes goes in the `output/lab06/` folder of the course project. `sdm.output_dir()` creates the folder and returns its path. Paths in Python are `Path` objects, and the `/` operator joins path pieces, e.g. `out_dir / "asciiRasters"`. ::: {#5059c888 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} env_stack = sdm.load_env() out_dir = sdm.output_dir("lab06") ascii_dir = sdm.output_dir("lab06", "asciiRasters") sdm.output_dir("lab06", "maxentOutput") # an empty folder for the Java app's results print(out_dir) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` C:\Users\rah\fw532-build\output\lab06 ``` ::: ::: Write out these rasters for Maxent to use. This takes a few seconds. The `for` loop runs the indented line once for each layer name, and `f"{name}.asc"` (an *f-string*) puts the name into the file name. ::: {#23c9287a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Write them back out in a new directory in ascii format for name in env_stack.names: sdm.write_ascii_grid(env_stack[name], env_stack, ascii_dir / f"{name}.asc") sorted(p.name for p in ascii_dir.glob("*.asc")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['Annual.Mean.Temperature.asc', 'Annual.Precipitation.asc', 'Isothermality.asc', 'Max.Temperature.of.Warmest.Month.asc', 'Mean.Diurnal.Range.asc', 'Mean.Temperature.of.Coldest.Quarter.asc', 'Mean.Temperature.of.Driest.Quarter.asc', 'Mean.Temperature.of.Warmest.Quarter.asc', 'Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter.asc', 'Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month.asc', 'Precipitation.Seasonality.asc', 'Precipitation.of.Coldest.Quarter.asc', 'Precipitation.of.Driest.Month.asc', 'Precipitation.of.Driest.Quarter.asc', 'Precipitation.of.Warmest.Quarter.asc', 'Precipitation.of.Wettest.Month.asc', 'Precipitation.of.Wettest.Quarter.asc', 'Temperature.Annual.Range.asc', 'Temperature.Seasonality.asc', 'elevation.asc'] ``` ::: ::: An `.asc` file is plain text: a six-line header, then one line of numbers per row of the raster. Here is the header of one of them: ::: {#e9e49f2b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} with open(ascii_dir / "elevation.asc") as f: for i in range(6): print(f.readline(), end="") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ncols 691 nrows 385 xllcorner -167.6666666667 yllcorner 7.1666666667 cellsize 0.1666666667 NODATA_value -9999 ``` ::: ::: The header gives the number of columns and rows, the coordinates of the lower-left corner, the cell size (in degrees), and the code for missing values (ocean cells). Maxent requires all the layers to have identical headers, which ours do because they come from one raster stack. Values are written with 6 significant digits. # Simulate Data We will use simulated data again in the exercises below. This is the same virtual species as in Lab 1 (and the same random seeds, so the same sites). ::: {#45fe802c .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # define logistic function def logistic(x): return np.exp(x) / (1 + np.exp(x)) # get points n_points = 1000 sim_pts = env_stack.sample_random(n_points, seed=1234) # set parameters intercept = -1.5 beta1 = -1.5 beta2 = -1.5 beta3 = 1.5 p_occ = logistic(intercept + beta1 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Precipitation.Seasonality"]) # 15 + beta2 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month"]) # 6 + beta3 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"])) # 8 # get the values that correspond to the points we selected: p_occs = sdm.extract(p_occ, env_stack, sim_pts["x"], sim_pts["y"]) # sample from these probabilities (with a *different* seed; see Lab 1): rng = np.random.default_rng(5678) pres_abs = rng.binomial(n=1, p=p_occs) # put response and variables together in a DataFrame: modeling_df = sim_pts.copy() modeling_df.insert(0, "presAbs", pres_abs) # plot the result is_pres = pres_abs == 1 ax = sdm.plot_map(p_occ, env_stack, title="pOcc") ax.scatter(sim_pts.loc[is_pres, "x"], sim_pts.loc[is_pres, "y"], s=6, color="red"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=531 height=292} ::: ::: Write these locations to a file for Maxent. Maxent wants three columns, in this order: the species name, the x coordinate (longitude), and the y coordinate (latitude). ::: {#915ab67a .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(is_pres.sum(), "of the", n_points, "sites are presences") pres_file = pd.DataFrame({"species": "simSpp", "x": sim_pts.loc[is_pres, "x"], "y": sim_pts.loc[is_pres, "y"]}) pres_file.to_csv(out_dir / "simSppPres.csv", index=False) pd.read_csv(out_dir / "simSppPres.csv").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 275 of the 1000 sites are presences ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
species x y

``` ::: ::: # Maxent At this point, switch over to the Java app to run Maxent on these data. > **Where are the files?** Everything Maxent needs is now in the `output/lab06/` folder of your > course project (the full path is printed in the set-up cell above). In the Maxent window: > > * **Samples:** `output/lab06/simSppPres.csv` > * **Environmental layers:** the folder `output/lab06/asciiRasters` (choose the folder itself, not > the files inside it). All 20 layers are continuous. > * **Output directory:** the empty folder `output/lab06/maxentOutput` > * **Test sample file** (on the Settings panel, for the section below): `output/lab06/simSppTestPres.csv` With the Java app, follow the Maxent tutorial using the data you generated through these sections: * Getting started * Doing a run * Looking at a prediction + In this section, try the suggestion in the tutorial to use a random seed for the test set. In addition, try supplying your own test set. Code to generate a test set for the simulated species is provided below. ::: {#8378bff2 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # same data generation with new random seeds test_pts = env_stack.sample_random(n_points, seed=4321) # get the probabilities that correspond to the points we selected: test_probs = sdm.extract(p_occ, env_stack, test_pts["x"], test_pts["y"]) # sample from these probabilities (again, a seed we haven't used yet): rng = np.random.default_rng(8765) test_resp = rng.binomial(n=1, p=test_probs) # plot the result is_test_pres = test_resp == 1 ax = sdm.plot_map(p_occ, env_stack, title="pOcc") ax.scatter(sim_pts.loc[is_pres, "x"], sim_pts.loc[is_pres, "y"], s=6, color="red", label="training presences") ax.scatter(test_pts.loc[is_test_pres, "x"], test_pts.loc[is_test_pres, "y"], s=6, color="blue", label="test presences") ax.legend(loc="lower left"); test_file = pd.DataFrame({"species": "simSpp", "x": test_pts.loc[is_test_pres, "x"], "y": test_pts.loc[is_test_pres, "y"]}) test_file.to_csv(out_dir / "simSppTestPres.csv", index=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=531 height=292} ::: ::: Note that Maxent stores the predictions for these test points in an output file that ends with samplePredictions.csv in the output directory. You could read these back into Python (with `pd.read_csv()`) for further processing/evaluation if desired. Continue through the tutorial sections: * Output formats + Create plots of each of the output formats for the simulated species. * Statistical analysis > **Question:** **Suggested discussion point:** Describe each output format: what it shows and how > they differ. Which seems most useful to you, in what context? In the next sections, you will do some model interpretation. Since you are working with simulated data, you KNOW which variables should show up as important and what their relationships to the prediction should be. In this example with all variables, you may find that the Maxent output doesn't represent the model you used to simulate the data very well. > **Question:** **Suggested discussion question:** Why might this be the case? How do the results > change if you ONLY include the relevant predictors? with just one irrelevant predictor that is > minimally correlated with the true variables? with only linear features (since the true model is > linear)? > **Exercise:** Do the following four sections of the tutorial with different settings to explore > these questions. > > * Which variables matter most? > * How does the prediction depend on the variables? > * Feature types and response curves > * Interactive exploration of predictions There is SO much more we could do, but we'll stop there for now. Browse through the rest of the tutorial to get a sense of what else it offers for future reference! ## Note: Supplying your own background points to deal with sampling bias One other thing you may want to do with Maxent is to supply your own background points instead of having them sampled randomly from the rasters you provide. You might do this if you want your background points to reflect the same sampling bias as the presence points (see the Phillips et al (2009) reference at the bottom of this lab) so the bias 'factors out.' The background could be drawn from a known sampling effort distribution (or this could be provided to the Maxent software as a bias file), or from opportunistic records of similar species that were likely sampled with the same bias (i.e. an empirical sample from the effort distribution). You could simulate this by sampling background data from the rasters above in Python, similarly to how we sampled presences (but without consulting the probability of occurrence). To supply background points to the Java app, you need to use the SWD format (a section of the tutorial we didn't get to). (In R, you can also supply them through the dismo::maxent interface using its 'a' argument.) Finally, the 'elapid' package (below) requires background points, even if they are randomly sampled. # Running with the 'elapid' package elapid does not include ALL the functions of the Java version. But, it may be nice sometimes to run Maxent within Python for comparison with other approaches or for other processing. elapid's `MaxentModel` follows the approach of the R package maxnet (Phillips et al. 2017): it builds the same kinds of features (linear, quadratic, product, hinge, threshold) and fits Maxent as a logistic regression of presences vs. background points in which each background point gets a large weight (100). A few differences from maxnet (the R version of this lab) are worth knowing: * elapid's defaults are different (linear, hinge, and product features; `beta_multiplier=1.5`), so below we set `feature_types` and `beta_multiplier` to match maxnet's defaults for 80 or more presences (linear, quadratic, product, hinge; regularization multiplier 1). * By default elapid fits the model with scikit-learn's L1-penalized (lasso) logistic regression, using one penalty for all features. maxnet (and the Java app) give each feature its own penalty. elapid uses 10 hinge knots per variable, maxnet 50. So expect similar, but not identical, results. # Simulate presence-background data for elapid We use the same seeds as above for the sites (1234) and the coin flips (5678), so these are the same presences you gave the Java app. The background points get a seed of their own. ::: {#cefabce5 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # define logistic function def logistic(x): return np.exp(x) / (1 + np.exp(x)) # get points n_points = 1000 n_background = 2000 sim_pts = env_stack.sample_random(n_points, seed=1234) background = env_stack.sample_random(n_background, seed=2468) # set parameters intercept = -1.5 beta1 = -1.5 beta2 = -1.5 beta3 = 1.5 p_occ = logistic(intercept + beta1 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Precipitation.Seasonality"]) + beta2 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month"]) + beta3 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"])) # get the values that correspond to the points we selected: p_occs = sdm.extract(p_occ, env_stack, sim_pts["x"], sim_pts["y"]) # sample from these probabilities: rng = np.random.default_rng(5678) pres = rng.binomial(n=1, p=p_occs) # put response and variables together in a DataFrame # (pd.concat stacks the presence rows on top of the background rows): pred_vars = env_stack.names # the 20 environmental variables modeling_df = pd.concat([sim_pts[pres == 1].assign(presBkgrnd=1), background.assign(presBkgrnd=0)], ignore_index=True) # plot the result ax = sdm.plot_map(p_occ, env_stack, title="pOcc") ax.scatter(background["x"], background["y"], s=4, color="blue") ax.scatter(sim_pts.loc[pres == 1, "x"], sim_pts.loc[pres == 1, "y"], s=4, color="red"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=531 height=292} ::: ::: Here is a demo with the main elapid functions. This is on the whole modeling DataFrame, so you can consider predicting to independent test data as an exercise (optional). To change the settings, use `beta_multiplier` (the regularization multiplier) and `feature_types` (e.g. `["linear", "quadratic"]`). `transform="cloglog"` sets the output format of `predict()` (the other options are `"raw"` and `"logistic"`). ::: {#06432bfe .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} maxent_model = elapid.MaxentModel(feature_types=["linear", "quadratic", "product", "hinge"], beta_multiplier=1.0, transform="cloglog", random_state=42) # the fitting algorithm uses random numbers too maxent_model.fit(modeling_df[pred_vars], modeling_df["presBkgrnd"]) n_used = np.sum(maxent_model.beta_scores_ != 0) print(n_used, "of", len(maxent_model.beta_scores_), "features have non-zero coefficients") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 94 of 590 features have non-zero coefficients ``` ::: ::: Response curves. To mirror maxnet's `plot()`, we vary one variable at a time over its range (plus 10% on each side) and hold all the other variables at their mean over the presence and background points. (elapid also has `maxent_model.partial_dependence_plot(X)`, which instead *averages* the predictions over all the rows of `X`, a partial dependence plot; we'll meet those in a later lab.) ::: {#9596f3d6 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} def response_curve(model, data, var, transform="cloglog", n=100): """Predictions along one variable, with the other variables held at their means.""" sweep = pd.DataFrame([data.mean()] * n) # n copies of the row of means lo, hi = data[var].min(), data[var].max() sweep[var] = np.linspace(lo - 0.1 * (hi - lo), hi + 0.1 * (hi - lo), n) if transform == "link": # the linear predictor = log of the raw output model.set_params(transform="raw") preds = np.log(model.predict(sweep)) else: model.set_params(transform=transform) preds = model.predict(sweep) model.set_params(transform="cloglog") # back to our default return sweep[var], preds fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 5, figsize=(15, 11), constrained_layout=True) for ax, var in zip(axes.flat, pred_vars): xs, preds = response_curve(maxent_model, modeling_df[pred_vars], var) ax.plot(xs, preds, color="black") ax.set_ylim(0, 1) ax.set_xlabel(var, fontsize=8) ax.set_ylabel("cloglog") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=1451 height=1067} ::: ::: Individual effects: ::: {#7acf807b .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} xs, preds = response_curve(maxent_model, modeling_df[pred_vars], "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter", transform="link") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5)) ax.plot(xs, preds, color="black") ax.set_xlabel("Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter") ax.set_ylabel("link (the linear predictor)"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=603 height=394} ::: ::: Prediction function example, but used on the same data that the model was fitted on. (pROC in the R version plots specificity on a reversed x-axis; here we plot the false positive rate, 1 − specificity, so the curves look the same.) ::: {#e612bf1a .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} maxent_preds = maxent_model.predict(modeling_df[pred_vars]) fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(modeling_df["presBkgrnd"], maxent_preds) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5)) ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color="black") ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="grey", linestyle="--") ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate (1 - specificity)") ax.set_ylabel("True positive rate (sensitivity)") ax.set_aspect("equal") print("AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(modeling_df["presBkgrnd"], maxent_preds), 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC: 0.7858 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-2.png){width=439 height=431} ::: ::: Note that this AUC compares presences with *background* points, not absences (some background points fall where the species is present), and it is computed on the training data. We can also predict to every cell and compare the predicted map with the truth: ::: {#b643e655 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = env_stack.to_frame() # one row per land cell maxent_map = env_stack.to_map(maxent_model.predict(grid[pred_vars]), index=grid.index) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4), constrained_layout=True) sdm.plot_map(p_occ, env_stack, ax=axes[0], title="True probability of occurrence", vmin=0, vmax=1) sdm.plot_map(maxent_map, env_stack, ax=axes[1], title="elapid prediction (cloglog)", vmin=0, vmax=1); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab06-maxent_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=1354 height=372} ::: ::: Compare where the prediction is high and low, rather than the values themselves. Presence-only data can't tell a model how common the species is (prevalence is not identifiable), so the cloglog scale rests on an assumption rather than on the data. # Turn in **(on Canvas, by the due date on Canvas)** Please post to the online discussion of this lab. Please include brief descriptions of your exploration of the exercises, with any relevant plots. Please also include, if applicable: * Any key take-aways from this lab that you want to remember for any future projects you may conduct in which you use species distribution models. * Any remaining questions or confusions do you have that you might like to learn more about. # Further Resources See the tutorials and papers linked from the software page at the top of the lab.
